source_review.notes: Checked all twelve structured references. Current Kubernetes Service, EndpointSlice, DNS, dual-stack, virtual-IP, Ingress, and NetworkPolicy documentation supports selectors, ports, exposure types, headless discovery, endpoint conditions/topology, A/AAAA/SRV records, IP-family policies, frozen Ingress status, path/TLS/class behavior, independent ingress/egress isolation, and implementation limits. Current Gateway API documentation supports HTTPRoute parents/matches/backends/status, role separation, listener attachment, conformance, conflict behavior, and target-side ReferenceGrant consent. No API status or control-plane resource is treated as proof of data-plane reachability, workload identity, authorization, end-to-end TLS, or user success.

evidence: Checked N=(C,E,D,R,B,T,A,P,O,L,X), selector-derived set S_t, serving/terminating/ready functions, request-hop sequence H, and topology request/capacity variables.
Checked tuple, set comprehension, models relation, conjunction, negation, ordered sequence, comparison, and indexed-variable syntax with the repository GitHub-math validator.
notation_and_syntax.notes: Selection, endpoint eligibility, route path, topology capacity, identity, and application success remain distinct.

evidence: Executed service-endpoint-eligibility and reproduced seven endpoints, six serving, four normal ready, two terminating, five IPv4, two IPv6, and three zones.
Recomputed normal readiness as serving and not terminating for addresses 10.0.0.1, 10.0.1.1, 2001:db8::1, and 10.0.2.2.
numerical_recomputation.notes: The fixture is synthetic and disclaims ownership, port, publication, propagation, reachability, and application equivalence.

evidence: Expanded the eleven-element connectivity contract through consumer/protocol, endpoints, discovery, routing, boundary, topology, security, policy, observation, lifecycle, and exceptions.
Expanded selector membership separately from readiness and authorization, and normal endpoint readiness separately from special publish-not-ready/consumer behavior.
Expanded the ordered request path and verified that every required layer is conjunctive for end-to-end success while one accepted layer is insufficient.
Checked same-zone preference against local request/capacity imbalance and fallback rather than treating locality as guaranteed availability.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: The notation models layered obligations and does not prove network reachability or security.

evidence: Reviewed zero/overmatched selectors, named-port drift, all-unready and terminating-only endpoints, publish-not-ready, stale EndpointSlices/DNS/connection pools, and manual EndpointSlice spoofing.
Reviewed Local-policy empty nodes, NAT/source loss, affinity abuse, topology imbalance, missing domain labels, zone failure, partial dual-stack paths, and provider-specific health/lifecycle.

Reviewed absent/wrong IngressClass, implementation-specific paths/annotations, route conflict, unaccepted/unprogrammed parents, cross-namespace confused deputy, ReferenceGrant revocation, and status information leakage.

Reviewed TLS hostname/expiry/reload/backend plaintext, broad Secret access, public abuse, additive NetworkPolicy gaps, NAT/host-network behavior, slow drain, persistent connections, force cleanup, and leaked provider resources.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: Selection, routing, topology, provider, namespace, security, drain, and cleanup behavior remain explicit under failure and attack.

evidence: Traced consumer/protocol intent through Service selection/ports, EndpointSlices, discovery, exposure, topology, Ingress/Gateway attachment, TLS/identity, NetworkPolicy, application, drain, and cleanup.

Checked exact selectors/ports, separate serving/terminating readiness, discovery-versus-identity, owned public exposure, capable headless clients, explicit Ingress class, Gateway role separation, and target-side consent.
Checked documented TLS hops, independent bidirectional network policy, dual-stack path evidence, propagation-aware drain, provider lifecycle, and control/data/application outcome separation.
invariant_checking.notes: All declared connectivity, ownership, security, topology, lifecycle, and evidence invariants hold across examples and answers.

proof_review.notes: The chapter states no theorem and contains no deductive proof.

proof_sketch_labeling.notes: No proof sketch is claimed; end-to-end success and security assumptions remain explicit.

evidence: The endpoint classifier is labeled synthetic and disclaims control/data/application equivalence.
Normative project documentation and practitioner synthesis remain distinguishable.
Worked examples are scenarios rather than production traffic, security, latency, or availability measurements.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: No external conformance test, penetration test, provider audit, traffic study, or production rollout is claimed.

conceptual_review.notes: The chapter consistently separates stable discovery, endpoint derivation, data-plane realization, exposure, topology, route ownership, TLS identity, network authorization, application handling, and user outcome.

practitioner_review.notes: A practitioner can design Service/EndpointSlice contracts, choose exposure and headless discovery, configure locality/dual stack, use portable Ingress, establish Gateway API roles and grants, map TLS hops, enforce NetworkPolicy, govern public routes, diagnose by layer, and test lifecycle.

pedagogical_review.notes: The sequence progresses from consumer/protocol through endpoints, Services, discovery, exposure, topology, dual stack, Ingress, Gateway, grants, policy, TLS, drain, governance, and diagnosis. Ten examples remain distinct; five exercises progress from connectivity design through audit, shared gateway, diagnosis, and emergency-network transfer, with complete answers.

limitations: Internal evidence record only; no external academic or practitioner review is claimed.
